This lecture, the second in the SmartUp Foundations Course, centers on the principle of "Branding First" — the idea that entrepreneurs should invest in building a brand before pouring resources into product development. Yonatan Stern, founder of ZoomInfo and the SmartUp Academy, challenges the common startup assumption that "if you build it, they will come," referencing the movie Field of Dreams to illustrate how dangerously naive that mindset can be. He argues that most entrepreneurs he meets have spent vast sums proving they can write code, when they should instead be directing that money toward establishing a recognizable brand that attracts customers organically.

Stern explains that branding differs from marketing in both scope and strategic value. A strong brand lowers customer acquisition costs because potential buyers come to you rather than requiring expensive cold outreach. It also clarifies who your ideal customers are, since engaged audiences effectively raise their hands. Perhaps most importantly, the branding process itself reshapes how founders think about their companies, often revealing overlooked revenue streams and prompting early, low-cost pivots — avoiding the classic startup trap of spending millions before realizing the original idea missed the mark.

The lecture draws heavily on real-world case studies. Stern recounts how ZoomInfo, founded in 2000 with modest financing, grew by publishing its people-and-company database as a free online directory — a bold SEO-driven branding move that generated massive organic traffic from salespeople and recruiters searching by name, title, and company. This long-tail SEO strategy turned ZoomInfo into a well-known brand before LinkedIn even had a comparable directory.

A second extended example features TickChak (TickShack), an Israeli events platform that built its brand by creating rich, SEO-optimized pages for thousands of artists and venues. Stern outlines a model where artists receive free homepages with updated show information and fan databases, while TickChak monetizes through low-cost communication tools — SMS fan engagement, pre-sales to loyal followers, and last-minute ticket promotions. He notes that a similar US company, Songkick, raised $61 million yet ultimately stagnated, underscoring that smart branding on a modest budget can outperform heavily funded competitors.

The overarching lesson is clear: branding is not a luxury or an afterthought — it is the foundation upon which profitable, fast-growing companies are built, and it should begin on day one.
